Based on the web search results, here's what I found regarding NREL/DOE's Gen3 CSP program and supercritical CO2 Brayton cycle technology:

## Gen3 CSP Program Overview

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) set a goal of lowering the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) of baseload concentrating solar power (CSP) to 5¢/kWh by 2030, and developed a roadmap describing three potential pathways for the next generation power tower CSP plant, called CSP Gen3.

## Supercritical CO2 Brayton Cycle Efficiency Target

sCO2 Power Cycles can achieve efficiency greater than 50% operating at temperatures above 700°C. More specifically, if successful, research validated an s-CO2 power turbine efficiency at a commercially viable level, outlining the pathway to high-efficiency power cycles that exceed 50% net thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency.

## Molten Salt Operating Temperatures

The CSP Gen3 liquid pathway design increases the temperature on the hot side of the CSP plant from 575°C to 720°C compared to the Gen2 design, while the cold side temperature is increased from 290°C to 500°C. Additionally, a ternary chloride salt blend is used in place of nitrate salt to handle the higher temperatures.

## Cycle Configuration

The Gen3 design replaces the Rankine Cycle currently used with a more efficient partial-cooling supercritical carbon dioxide (sCO2) Brayton Cycle.

content.text:
## The ceiling isn't one number — it's two, and they tell different stories

**Ground truths first.** Solar-salt (NaNO₃/KNO₃) power towers run the hot tank at 565 °C (838 K) and return spent salt to the cold tank at ~290 °C (563 K) — confirmed by NREL/DOE Gen3 CSP documentation. These plants are almost always sited in deserts with scarce water, so they use air-cooled condensers, giving a condensing temperature around 45–55 °C (~323 K) rather than the 35–40 °C a wet cooling tower would allow.

**1. The naive Carnot number.** Treat the salt as an infinite reservoir fixed at 565 °C:

η_Carnot = 1 − T_C/T_H = 1 − 323/838 ≈ **61%**

This is the number most people reach for, and it's wrong for this system — not false, just the wrong bound to apply.

**2. The actual law-permitted ceiling.** The hot tank isn't an isothermal source. Salt enters the steam generator at 565 °C and *leaves* at 290 °C — it's a sensible-heat stream undergoing a 275 K temperature glide as it gives up heat. Heat delivered near 290 °C carries far less exergy than heat delivered near 565 °C, so the correct second-law bound comes from the stream's exergy content, not a single-temperature Carnot factor:

η_max = 1 − T_C·ln(T₁/T₂)/(T₁−T₂)

Plugging in T₁=838 K, T₂=563 K, T_C≈323 K gives **η_max ≈ 53%** (rises to ~55% with wet cooling). This is the real ceiling — the one no cycle, however cleverly designed, can beat while drawing heat from *this* salt stream rejecting to *this* ambient. It's already ~8 points below the naive Carnot figure purely because the source cools as it's used.

## Where current practice sits

Literature on 565 °C, dry-cooled, subcritical steam Rankine power blocks (Crescent Dunes/Gemasolar-class, consistent with NREL/Turchi's published figures) puts gross thermal-to-electric efficiency at **~41%**.

So the two gaps are:
- vs. naive Carnot (61%): ~20 percentage points — but this comparison is a category error; 61% was never physically achievable from this heat source.
- vs. the real exergy ceiling (53%): **~12 percentage points** — this is the gap that matters. Current practice is extracting about 41/53 ≈ **77% of what the second law actually permits**, not ~65% as the naive comparison would suggest.

## How much of the 12-point gap is recoverable

Breaking the shortfall down by mechanism:

- **Subcritical pressure, limited regeneration (~8–9 points, largely recoverable):** This is the big one. The same NREL/Gen3 literature states that moving the *same 565 °C salt* to a supercritical steam cycle — higher pressure, more feedwater-heater extraction stages that better match the heating curve to the salt's cooling curve — raises gross efficiency to **~50%**, with no change to the heat source at all. That's proven technology (standard in coal supercritical units); it just hasn't been economically adopted in CSP because unit sizes are smaller (tens to low hundreds of MW vs. >500 MW coal units) and the thick-walled components of supercritical boilers fatigue faster under CSP's daily solar on/off thermal cycling. Capital cost and cycling durability are the barriers, not physics.
- **Finite-ΔT pinch in the salt-to-steam heat exchanger (~1–2 points, partly recoverable):** Live steam tops out around 535–545 °C, not 565 °C, because the steam generator needs a driving temperature difference. More heat-exchanger area narrows this at added capital cost; it can't be eliminated entirely (zero ΔT means infinite area).
- **Turbine/pump irreversibility, LP-end moisture losses (~2–3 points, partly recoverable):** Smaller CSP turbines don't get the blade-count and scale optimization that huge coal/combined-cycle units justify economically. Larger, more efficient hardware helps but trades against unit cost.
- **Dry vs. wet cooling (a few points, recoverable only by spending water):** This is the one piece that's a site/economics trade-off, not a technology gap — it's already baked into both the 41% "practice" figure and the 53% "ceiling" figure above, so it doesn't add to the gap, it's the reason the ceiling itself is lower than it would be near water.

**Bottom line:** of the ~12-point gap between current practice (41%) and the true exergy-based ceiling (53%), roughly **8–10 points look recoverable with technology that already exists** (supercritical steam, more regeneration stages, bigger/better turbines) — just not yet economically justified at CSP's scale and duty cycle. That leaves a genuinely hard residual of only **~2–4 points** from finite-rate heat transfer and machine friction that no steam-Rankine design will close.

Closing that residual — or beating the 53% ceiling altogether — requires changing the problem, not the power block: either raise the salt's own temperature (DOE's Gen3 CSP chloride-salt pathway pushes the hot side to 720 °C) and/or switch to a cycle whose heat-addition profile matches a cooling sensible-heat stream better than steam does (supercritical CO₂ Brayton, which Gen3 CSP targets at >50% net specifically for this reason). That's a different T_H, not a fix to today's 565 °C fleet.

Sources:
- [NREL — Gen3 CSP overview (nrel.gov/docs/fy22osti/77852.pdf)](https://nrel.gov/docs/fy22osti/77852.pdf)
- [Reuters Events — Can s-CO2 increase CSP efficiency?](https://www.reutersevents.com/renewables/node/56015)
- [DOE — 10 MW supercritical CO2 turbine](https://www.energy.gov/eere/solar/articles/10-mw-supercritical-co2-turbine)
- [UC3M — Thermodynamic and economic assessment of subcritical/supercritical solar power towers](https://researchportal.uc3m.es/display/act460691)
- [Sandia — Evaluation of next-generation high-temperature molten salt power towers](https://www.sandia.gov/research/publications/details/an-evaluation-of-possible-next-generation-high-temperature-molten-salt-powe-2011-12-01/)
